subject: Chemistry
title: Isotopes: Same Element, Different Weight
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Isotopes: Same Element, Different Weight.

hook.text: Carbon-12 and Carbon-14 are the same element with the same chemistry—but different masses. They're isotopes.

buildup.text: Isotopes have the same number of protons (same element) but different numbers of neutrons (different mass).

discovery.text: Frederick Soddy discovered isotopes in 1913 while studying radioactive decay chains of thorium and uranium.

twist.text: Carbon-14 is radioactive with a half-life of 5,730 years. Archaeologists use it to date ancient objects up to 50,000 years old.

climax.text: Hydrogen has three isotopes: protium (0 neutrons), deuterium (1 neutron), and tritium (2 neutrons, radioactive).

punchline.text: Same protons, different neutrons. Same chemistry, different stability.

quiz.question: What makes two atoms isotopes of the same element?
options: Same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
Same number of electrons but different protons
Same atomic mass but different chemical properties

details.summary: Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have identical proton counts but different numbers of neutrons, giving them different atomic masses. Frederick Soddy coined the term in 1913, and isotopes explain why atomic weights are not whole numbers on the periodic table.
details.whyItMatters: Isotopes are essential for radiocarbon dating, medical imaging, nuclear energy, and understanding stellar nucleosynthesis. They reveal that elements are families, not single entities.
takeaways: Isotopes share the same proton count but differ in neutron count
Non-integer atomic weights reflect natural isotope mixtures
Some isotopes are stable while others undergo radioactive decay

faq.question: How many isotopes does a typical element have?
faq.answer: Most elements have between two and ten stable or long-lived isotopes. Tin has the most stable isotopes at ten. Some elements like gold naturally exist as only one isotope. Including radioactive isotopes, many elements have dozens of known variants.

faq.question: Why do isotopes of the same element behave chemically the same?
faq.answer: Chemical behavior is determined by electron configuration, which depends on proton count. Since isotopes have the same number of protons and electrons, they undergo identical chemical reactions. Differences in mass affect physical properties like diffusion rates but not chemical bonding.
